Graph-Native Infrastructure for Context and Accountable AI Systems

Developer-first, knowledge infrastructure for AI, alternative to expensive enterprise platforms.

Ingest your enterprise data, extract what matters, build a Context Graph and knowledge graph (KG), and run graph analytics and causal reasoning over all of it, with full decision provenance baked in. Explainable, traceable, and trustworthy by design.

Context Management · Knowledge Modeling · Deterministic Reasoning · Ontology Management · Decision Intelligence · End-to-End Traceability

Open Source · Governed · Zero Vendor Lock-In

Polyglot Graph Storage · RDF & LPG Support · W3C Standards · Interoperable

Built for High-Stakes, Regulated Domains

pip install semantica

English · Deutsch · Français · Español · Italiano · Português · العربية · اردو · हिन्दी · 中文 · 日本語 · 한국어

Knowledge Explorer · Context Graphs · Reasoning Engine · Decision Intelligence · Ontology Hub

▶ Watch the full platform walkthrough

Most AI agents run on embeddings, not meaning: similarity scores with no structure, no relationships, and no way to explain why a result came back.

Semantica is the semantic/context layer underneath your LLM, vector store, and agent framework: deterministic infrastructure (no LLM required for graph construction, reasoning, or provenance; where an LLM is used, it's optional and vendor-neutral, every major provider supported, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and more, via semantica.llms ) that turns fragmented enterprise data into a structured, queryable Context Graph and knowledge graph that carries the business context, not just the data structure. Ontologies and controlled vocabularies (OWL, SHACL, SKOS) make what an entity means to your business, its definitions, relationships, and rules, as explicit as the data itself, not just its embedding.

Decision provenance and audit trails aren't the product. They fall out of that structure for free, and in domains a regulator can question, the same structure that makes your agent smarter also gives you a straight answer to "why."

System-level explainability, not foundation-model explainability. Semantica doesn't expose or reconstruct what happens inside the LLM: its internal reasoning stays opaque, like it does for any external system. Semantica explains what's outside the model: the context fed in, the decision produced, its provenance, relevant relationships, applied policies, and the full execution trail.

Who it's for:

AI/ML platform teams shipping agents that make consequential decisions and need structured, queryable context, not just a vector index

Enterprise data teams on Databricks, Snowflake, or SAP turning tables already in the lakehouse or warehouse into a governed, lineage-tracked knowledge graph, without exporting to a third-party SaaS

Compliance, risk, and audit teams who need a straight answer to "why did the AI do that?" in a format a regulator accepts

Regulated enterprises (finance, healthcare, legal, government, defense) that can't ship a black box or hand their data to someone else's SaaS to get one

Platform and infra engineers who want the KG, reasoning, and provenance stack self-hosted and swappable, not locked to one vendor's backend

Data and knowledge engineers building a KG from messy, multi-source data, where conflicting facts get flagged and duplicates get merged, not silently overwritten

Quick Start · Architecture · What You Get · Why Semantica · Decision Intelligence · Context Graphs · Recipe: Audit Trail · Module Reference · Integrations · CLI · Performance · Install

What Semantica Gives You

Context Graphs: A structured, queryable graph of everything your agent knows, decides, and reasons about

Decision Intelligence: Every decision is a first-class object: traceable, searchable by precedent, and causally linked

AI Governance & Ontology: SHACL constraints, conflict detection, compliance rules, OWL generation, and SKOS vocabularies, all with a visual editor

Full Auditability: W3C PROV-O provenance on every fact, exportable to JSON, CSV, or RDF

Deterministic Reasoning: Forward chaining, Rete network, Datalog, and SPARQL, with fully explainable paths, not black boxes

Knowledge Pipeline: Multi-source ingestion, entity-aware chunking, NER/relation/event extraction, and graph construction, with semantic dedup and provenance-preserving merges built in

Enterprise Data Platforms: Native connectors for Databricks (Unity Catalog + Delta Lake), Snowflake, and SAP OData, so data already in your lakehouse or warehouse becomes graph nodes with provenance, no export/import hop

Graph Analytics: Centrality, community detection, link prediction, and shortest-path queries over the graph you just built

实况照片（Live Photo） ：抖音和小红书统一由 config/base_config.py 中的 DOWNLOAD_LIVE_PHOTO 控制，默认 True ，仅在 ENABLE_GET_MEDIA 开启时生效。设为 False 后只保存静态图，普通视频下载不受影响。实况视频与静态图使用相同的原始图片序号（如 001.jpg / 001_live.mp4 ），缺失媒体时保留序号空位。这里保存的是独立图片与随附视频，不合成手机相册的 Live Photo，也不转换为 GIF。小红书 Web 返回的实况视频可能自带水印，下载会保留该视频的原始内容。

Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness

<a id="user-content-prime-agent-a-self-improving-rlm-harness" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink:

Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness

" href="#prime-agent-a-self-improving-rlm-harness">

Documentation •

Prime Agent is an open-source coding and research agent for general and long-running work. It is designed around two core abstractions:

The Recursive Language Model (RLM) treats context as variables ( prompt-as-a-variable ) and tools like recursive subagents as function calls ( programmatic tool /sub-agent calling ) inside a persistent REPL.

The Continual Harness stores supplemental prompts, memories, skill descriptions, and reusable subagent specifications as durable state that Prime Agent can refine through small, evidence-backed updates, local to the session by default.

Install the latest stable version with the one-command installer:

curl -fsSL https://app.primeintellect.ai/prime-agent/install.sh | sh

On Windows, install from PowerShell:

irm https: // app.primeintellect.ai / prime - agent / install.ps1 | iex

The Windows installer downloads the latest stable Windows x64 build and verifies its checksum before installation.

Why Prime Agent

Prime Agent combines a persistent Python control environment with durable harness state, so useful working context and reusable operating patterns can outlive a single chat window.

Everything is programmatic: a persistent Python REPL is the built-in model tool; file operations, shell commands, tool use, subagents, and context management happen through code.

Subagents are built in: rlm.spawn(...) spawns real child agents for parallel or background work and returns their results programmatically.

The harness can improve: /refine reviews the current trajectory and can apply small, evidence-backed updates to supplemental harness state. It never rewrites the immutable base system prompt, and recorded snapshots support rollback.

Skills are executable: skills are importable Python packages, and the built-in skill creator can turn recurring workflows into project or personal skills.

Sessions run in the background: daemon-backed agents keep running when the terminal disconnects and can be reattached later.

Agents communicate directly: running agents can exchange messages and orchestrate one another without routing everything through the user.

Long tasks keep moving: automatic compaction, persistent goals, heartbeats, schedules, autonomous mode, and retained subagents preserve progress across turns and terminal sessions.

Connect Slack from /mcp or run /mcp login slack inside Prime Agent to search

your workspace and use Slack tools. See the Slack connector guide

for OAuth setup and troubleshooting.

Google Drive and Google Sheets

Connect Google's official Drive and Sheets MCP servers with your own Google

OAuth client: add them to mcpServers with clientId , clientSecret ,

callbackPort , and scopes , then run /mcp login <name> . See the

Google Drive and Google Sheets guide for the

Google Cloud setup and the tool mapping.

Clipboard over SSH and tmux

Prime Agent uses the local clipboard tool (such as pbcopy ) when available. In tmux it asks the attached tmux client to forward a clipboard buffer if that client advertises the Ms capability. This works with tmux's default set-clipboard external , unlike application-origin OSC 52. Without tmux, remote copies request delivery using OSC 52. Terminal requests cannot confirm that your local clipboard changed, so Prime Agent reports them as unconfirmed.

Nested tmux servers and terminals may still block delivery. An outer tmux with set-clipboard external can reject the inner server's OSC 52. In that case, run tmux set -s set-clipboard on on the outer server, or use native terminal selection (Shift-drag in most terminals; Option-drag in iTerm2) followed by Cmd-C. macOS Terminal.app does not support OSC 52; iTerm2 requires its “Applications in terminal may access clipboard” setting.

Custom certificate authorities

HTTPS requests trust your operating system's trust store together with the bundled Mozilla roots. For servers behind a custom CA, point NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS at a PEM bundle of your CA certificates — the same variable the Node/TypeScript build honors:

export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/to/your-ca.pem

Each transport reads the variable once when its first client is initialized. The background daemon keeps the environment it started with, so run prime-agent shutdown after changing it.

Getting Started

Start Prime Agent from the repository or directory you want it to work in:

<div class="highlight highlight-source-shell notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="cd /path/to/project

prime-agent"> cd /path/to/project

On first launch, run /login to choose a subscription or API-key provider. Prime Agent works in the current directory and can run commands and modify files there. Use a disposable clone, clean worktree, or another checkpoint you can inspect and restore.

π RuView is a WiFi sensing platform that turns radio signals into spatial intelligence.

Every WiFi router already fills your space with radio waves. When people move, breathe, or even sit still, they disturb those waves in measurable ways. RuView captures these disturbances using Channel State Information (CSI) from low-cost ESP32 sensors and turns them into actionable data: who's there, what they're doing, and whether they're okay.

What it senses:

Presence and occupancy — detect people through walls, count them, track entries and exits

Vital signs — breathing rate and heart rate, contactless, while sleeping or sitting

Activity recognition — walking, sitting, gestures, falls — from temporal CSI patterns

Environment mapping — RF fingerprinting identifies rooms, detects moved furniture, spots new objects

Sleep quality — overnight monitoring with sleep stage classification and apnea screening

Also included:

Camera-free pose — estimate 17 body keypoints from WiFi CSI

Built-in model workflow — record CSI, train models, load RVF files, and switch LoRA profiles

Local automation — HOMECORE provides state, history, automations, signed Wasm plugins, voice hooks, and HomeKit support

Unified RF world model — combine WiFi CSI, radar, UWB, and cellular sensing in one privacy-bounded scene model; accuracy is still synthetic until real-data validation

Governed evidence — attach privacy policy, uncertainty, provenance, and witness records to sensing events

The AI-Powered Life Operating System

Website · Install · Walkthrough · Docs · Releases

LifeOS-8.761.0-release.mp4

LifeOS is a General Purpose AI Harness for doing anything you want to do in life and work with AI. It captures who you are, what you care about, and where you're trying to go, then uses AI that knows you to help you get there.

And because it has your full context, it makes everything you do more efficient and effective, from building apps, to starting a business, to creative projects… basically anything .

The whole system works on one central concept: moving from your Current State to your Ideal State — in pursuit of Euphoric Surprise.

⭐ If LifeOS is useful to you, star the repo

Stars help more people find the project and keep it moving. It takes one click.

⚠️ Your Security Is Your Responsibility

LifeOS is fundamentally one person's personal AI harness, published as-is, and it is constantly in flux: security features are added, enhanced, removed, modified and adjusted from release to release. The security of any LifeOS component, and of the system as a whole, is not guaranteed. Responsibility for the security of your system is yours, not the LifeOS authors' or contributors'.

Before anything is installed, the installer asks: "Do you understand that you are responsible for the security of your own system and that we are not responsible?" It goes ahead only if you answer yes. See SECURITY.md .

Give it to your AI. LifeOS is installed by an AI, so the install is just a prompt. Paste this into your AI coding harness — Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Hermes, or any capable agent — and it does the whole setup for you:

Read https://ourlifeos.ai/install and install LifeOS for me.

Your AI reads the install page and walks the setup, asking permission before it touches anything.

Prefer the terminal? There's a one-line shortcut for Claude Code on macOS/Linux:

curl -fsSL https://ourlifeos.ai/install.sh | bash

Either path needs a capable AI coding harness — we build and run on Claude Code — and bun .

Core Components

The unique features — the parts you won't find anywhere else. Anything a good harness already provides on its own (built-in subagents, for example) isn't listed; this is only what LifeOS adds. See them live and click through on ourlifeos.ai .

LifeOS ships 97 public skills, from research, security, writing and art to video, publishing and your home. Browse them all on the site.

Browse all skills →

How is LifeOS different from using an AI harness on its own?

Your harness gives you raw capability. LifeOS is the layer on top that makes it yours — a system that knows your goals, people, and context, and keeps working toward them:

Persistent memory — Your DA remembers past sessions, decisions, and learnings

Custom skills — Specialized capabilities for the things you do most

Your context — Goals, contacts, preferences—all available without re-explaining

Intelligent routing — Say "research this" and the right workflow triggers automatically

Self-improvement — The system modifies itself based on what it learns

Your harness is the engine. LifeOS is everything else that makes it your car.

What harness does LifeOS run on?

Any high-end one. LifeOS is harness-agnostic by design — it's built on universal primitives (hooks, skills, context files, agentic routing), not one vendor's features. The code is TypeScript and Bash, and the core ideas — TELOS, the Algorithm, skills, memory — port to any capable agent.

Daniel builds and runs it on Claude Code , so that's the most-tested path today. But LifeOS isn't locked to it, and it's designed to run wherever your AI does.

How is this different from fabric?

Fabric is a collection of AI prompts (patterns) for specific tasks. It's focused on what to ask AI .

LifeOS is infrastructure for how your DA operates —memory, skills, routing, context, self-improvement. They're complementary. Many LifeOS users integrate Fabric patterns into their skills.

What if I break something?

Recovery is straightforward:

Back up first — Before any upgrade: cp -r ~/.claude ~/.claude-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d)

USER/ is safe — Your customizations in USER/ are never touched by the installer or upgrades

Settings merge, not overwrite — The installer only updates identity and version fields; your hooks, statusline, and custom config are preserved

Git-backed — Version control everything, roll back when needed

History is preserved — Your DA's memory survives mistakes

DA can fix it — Your DA helped build it, it can help repair it

Re-install — Run the installer again; it detects existing installations and merges intelligently

Local Model Support

Run LifeOS with local models (Ollama, llama.cpp) for privacy and cost control

Remote Access

Access your LifeOS from anywhere—mobile, web, other devices

Outbound Phone Calling

Voice capabilities for outbound calls

WeatherNext 2

This repo contains the code for WeatherNext 2 (WN2), the global, medium-range

atmospheric and cyclone forecasting model developed by Google DeepMind and

Google Research.

It also contains code for prior generation models

Accessing Forecast Data Feeds

If you are interested in directly accessing daily data feeds of WN2 model

outputs rather than running the model yourself, we provide them across multiple

Google Cloud

(including Earth Engine, BigQuery, and Vertex AI).

WeatherLab (including cyclone tracks).

OpenMeteo (including an API and interactive builder).

Model Guide & Documentation: Google Developers WeatherNext Guide

WeatherNext Cyclones Paper: Operational tropical cyclone forecasting

FGN/WN2 Technical Report: Skillful joint probabilistic weather

forecasting from marginals

(arXiv:2506.10772)

WeatherNext 2 Blog Post: WeatherNext 2: Our most advanced weather forecasting model

WeatherNext Cyclones Blog Post: WeatherNext: AI model achieves breakthrough in forecasting cyclones

Older Models

This repository serves as the primary home for the WeatherNext family models.

Alongside WN2, this repository also hosts the code and documentation for our

legacy and specialized models:

WeatherNext Graph : Deterministic

medium-range weather forecasting using graph neural networks. Published as

WeatherNext Gen : Diffusion-based ensemble

forecasting for medium-range weather. Published as GenCast.

Provided Pretrained Models

This repository provides code to run the different versions of WeatherNext 2 and

WeatherNext Cyclones. The only difference between them is that WN2 can also

predict 100m wind. In particular, WN2 also forecasts cyclones with the exact

same algorithm as WN Cyclones. Their weights are different due to independent

training runs.

WeatherNext 2

WeatherNext2_<2025 (Used Operationally): 0.25° resolution (~30km).

Fine-tuned on ECMWF HRES data and designed to be initialized directly from

operational HRES initial conditions rather than ERA5 reanalysis. Trained on

data through 2024. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNext2_<2025_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNext Cyclones - models which reproduce the results in paper

WeatherNextCyclones_<2025 (Used Operationally): 0.25° resolution. The

model that ran live during the 2025 Atlantic hurricane season, publicly

referred to as FNV3 (NHC's postprocessed version was called GDMI). Trained

on data through 2024. The paper appendix contains a partial evaluation of

2025 in NHC basins for this model checkpoint, and how the tracker

improvement in September 2025 improved results. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2025_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_<2024 : 0.25° resolution. Reproduces results from the

paper on 2024. Trained on data through 2023. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2024_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_<2023 : 0.25° resolution. Reproduces results from the

paper on 2023. Trained on data through 2022. Corresponding weights files:

WeatherNextCyclones_<2023_model{1,2,3,4}.npz .

WeatherNext Cyclones Mini

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2024 : 1° resolution. A lightweight version

suitable for lower memory and compute constraints (e.g., local testing or

single TPUs or GPUs). Not expected to match the performance of the larger

versions. Forecasts the same things as WeatherNext2_<2025, including

cyclones. Trained on data through 2023. Corresponding weights file:

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2024.npz .

WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2023 : As above, but only trained on data through

2022. Corresponding weights file: WeatherNextCyclones_Mini_<2023.npz .

Evaluation results for WeatherNextCyclones_Mini can be found in the appendix

WeatherNext Cyclones Paper .

Quick Start Guide

The easiest way to get started with WeatherNext 2 is by running our interactive

Colab Notebook , which can be opened from

Colaboratory .

This notebook defaults to WeatherNext Cyclones Mini, which we recommend running

using the v5e-1 runtime, available for free as a Colab runtime. However, the

notebook can also be used to run the other models enumerated above (but these

will require a v5p accelerator).

In general, we recommend running WeatherNext 2 on TPU where possible, since its

implementation has been optimised for it. However, if choosing to run on GPU,

the attention implementation must be switched, as shown in the demo notebook.

The non-Mini models require H100 for sufficient VRAM. The Mini models should

manage inference on a P100.

Pre-trained weights and sample data are available on our Google Cloud

Inside the notebook, you will learn how to:

Automatically load the required model weights from our storage bucket.

Load initial state weather data (e.g., HRES initial conditions).

Initialize the WN2 (FGN) architecture.

Run auto-regressive rollout steps to generate a forecast prediction.

Visualize the outputs (e.g., temperature, wind speed, geopotential height).

Run the direct tracker on model outputs to obtain track data for cyclones.

Compute the training loss on model predictions and targets, and take a

gradient step.

Installation

This is research code provided as-is for the purpose of running and

experimenting with the published models. There are no guarantees of API

stability and future updates may introduce breaking changes without notice. We

recommend pinning to a specific release.

pip install git+https://github.com/google-deepmind/weathernext.git@v0.3.0

Model Weights

To run WeatherNext 2 or WeatherNext Cyclones, you will need to download the

pre-trained model weights. You can access the weights on Google Cloud

Code-Graph-RAG

Code-Graph-RAG parses a multi-language codebase with Tree-sitter, sharpened by compiler-grade frontends and runtime traces where available, builds a knowledge graph of its structure in an embedded graph database that needs no server, and lets you query, edit, and optimise that code in plain English. It works across a monorepo of mixed languages under one unified graph schema.

1. Index: cgr start --update-graph parses a repository into a knowledge graph (sped up)

2. Ask: cgr start answers questions and edits code, grounded in that graph

Latest News 🔥

Type Handling : Improved handling of type context managers, walrus operators, and match binding targets in both Python and TypeScript.

Rename Refinement : Prevented Go renames from unexporting names used by other packages.

Profile Naming : Corrected the naming of pprof profiles to avoid "malformed" errors when no samples are present.

Output Budget : Increased the Anthropic output budget to improve the default thinking experience.

Module Resolution : Resolved issues with module resolution in various scenarios, including ES module default imports and bare name bindings.

Dead Code Elimination : Removed dead code roots associated with IPython rich-display methods.

Incremental Refresh : Improved incremental refresh to ensure callers are updated when dispatch targets change.

See NEWS.md for the full history.

What It Does

Point Code-Graph-RAG at a repository and it reads every source file, extracts functions, classes, methods, modules, and the relationships between them, and stores the result as an interconnected graph. Once the graph exists you can:

Ask questions about the codebase in natural language and get answers grounded in the real structure.

Retrieve the actual source of any function, class, or method by name or by intent.

Edit code through the agent with AST-based surgical patching and a diff preview before anything changes.

Optimise code against language best practices or your own coding standards.

Find dead code by walking call and reference edges from entry points.

Search and rewrite structurally by AST pattern with ast-grep.

Overlay runtime behaviour: trace a test run (or pull production eBPF profiles) with cgr trace and merge the calls that actually happened into the graph, exposing dispatch that static analysis cannot see.

How It Works

The system has two components:

Multi-language parser. A Tree-sitter based parser reads the codebase and ingests functions, classes, methods, modules, and their relationships into the graph under a single language-agnostic schema. Where a toolchain is available, compiler-grade frontends layer exact facts on top (libclang for C/C++, go/types for Go, and opt-in Roslyn, javac and Jedi for C#, Java and Python), and dynamic tracing merges calls observed at runtime. Tree-sitter stays the backbone: a trace only sees code that ran, and a compiler frontend only covers what its toolchain can build.

RAG system ( codebase_rag/ ). An interactive CLI that turns natural language into Cypher queries, retrieves matching code, and drives AI-powered editing and optimisation.

<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="Source Code -> Tree-sitter Parser -> AST Analysis -> Knowledge Graph

User Query -> AI Model (Cypher Gen) -> Cypher Query -> Graph Results -> Response"> Source Code -> Tree-sitter Parser -> AST Analysis -> Knowledge Graph

User Query -> AI Model (Cypher Gen) -> Cypher Query -> Graph Results -> Response

The graph is stored in an embedded SQLite file by default. Memgraph and Neo4j are opt-in backends that run the same Cypher; Graph Backends compares them.

See the Architecture Overview and Graph Schema for the full picture.

Supported Languages

Python, TypeScript, TSX, JavaScript, Rust, Go, Java, C, C++, C#, PHP, Lua, Dart, and Julia are fully supported. Scala is in development, and Ruby, Kotlin, Swift, Elixir, Haskell, Solidity, Bash, and Nix have structural support (modules, functions, classes where the language has them, and imports) through the pluggable ast-grep tier. See the Language Support matrix for per-language capabilities.

Installation

cgr is published to PyPI. Install it system-wide with the treesitter-full (tree-sitter grammars), ast-grep (Ruby, Kotlin, Swift, Elixir, Haskell, Solidity, Bash, Nix) and semantic (vector search) extras:

T3 Code is an "agent harness control surface". It enables control of the agents on your machine with a best-in-class mobile app ( iOS , Android ), web app and Electron-based desktop app .

Works with your subscriptions on Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, and fx. If they're set up on your computer, T3 Code can control them.

"Wait, what are you selling me?"

Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork and build the editor that you want.

Installation

T3 Code currently supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Antigravity, and fx. Install and authenticate at least one provider before use:

Codex: install Codex CLI and run codex login

Claude: install Claude Code and run claude auth login

Cursor: install Cursor CLI and run agent login

Grok Build: install Grok Build CLI and run grok login

OpenCode: install OpenCode and run opencode auth login

Antigravity: enable it in Settings, then use Install Antigravity and Sign in with Google . No CLI is required.

fx: install fx and run fx login on the machine running the T3 Code server ( setup guide )

Command line

curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https: // t3.codes / install.ps1 | iex

Then run t3 to start the server and open the local web app. t3 service install keeps it running in the background, t3 update moves to a newer release, and t3 --help has the full reference.

To try it once without installing, run npx t3@latest . It offers to install the t3 command for you.

Install the latest version of the desktop app from GitHub Releases , or from your favorite package registry:

Windows ( winget )

winget install T3Tools.T3Code

Windows ( scoop )

scoop install extras/t3code

macOS (Homebrew)

brew install --cask t3-code

Debian, Ubuntu ( .deb )

Download the .deb from GitHub Releases , then:

sudo apt install ./T3-Code- * .deb

Arch Linux (AUR)

yay -S t3code-bin

yay -S t3code-nightly-bin

The AUR packaging is maintained in this repository under packaging/aur .

Nix (nixpkgs)

nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code

The package is maintained in nixpkgs

and includes the desktop app ( t3code-desktop ) and the t3 command.

See Nix installation for NixOS configuration and updates.

We are very very early in this project. Expect bugs.

We are (mostly) not accepting contributions yet. Small fixes may be considered. Big features will not be.

items.title: Beans at altitude: stovetop vs. pressure cooker
items.summary: Beans at altitude: stovetop vs. pressure cooker（来源：Hacker News）
items.content:
Cooking beans at altitude is one of the clearest examples of how mountain conditions change everyday food science, because dried beans that soften predictably near sea level often stay tough, split unevenly, or take far longer once elevation lowers boiling temperature. In this cooking methods hub, “altitude” means locations generally above 3,000 feet, where atmospheric pressure drops enough to affect simmering, evaporation, and pressure differentials inside foods. “Stovetop” refers to conventional soaking and simmering in an open or partially covered pot, while “pressure cooker” includes stovetop and electric models that trap steam and raise the cooking temperature above the local boiling point. The distinction matters because beans depend on sustained heat, moisture, and time to gelatinize starches and dissolve pectins in their cell walls. I have tested pintos, black beans, chickpeas, and cannellini beans in both methods across elevations from roughly 5,000 to 8,000 feet, and the pattern is consistent: altitude magnifies small process errors. If you under-soak, salt too late, use old beans, or let the pot boil hard, the penalty grows. If you choose the right method, however, altitude does not stop you from getting creamy centers and intact skins. This article explains how each method works, where each shines, and how to decide which cooking path fits your kitchen and the bean dish you want.

Why altitude changes bean cooking

At higher elevations, water boils at a lower temperature than 212°F. Around 5,000 feet, boiling is close to 203°F, and by 7,500 feet it is lower still. Beans cooked in an open pot therefore simmer in cooler water, which slows starch gelatinization and softening of hemicellulose and pectin in the seed coat. That is why a pot of chickpeas that might finish in 90 minutes near sea level can take two to three hours in Denver or Santa Fe. Lower pressure also increases evaporation, so the water level drops faster and beans can become exposed, leading to uneven cooking and split skins.

Bean age matters even more at altitude. Old beans lose internal moisture over storage and can develop the hard-to-cook defect, especially when stored warm. Minerals in water also matter. Hard water high in calcium and magnesium can reinforce pectin structure and delay softening. Acids from tomatoes, vinegar, wine, or molasses likewise slow softening if added early. Salt is different: despite old kitchen myths, salting the soaking water or early cooking water generally improves flavor and can help beans cook more evenly by seasoning the interior. The practical takeaway is simple: at altitude, method choice is important, but ingredient handling is just as important.

Stovetop beans at altitude: strengths, limits, and best uses

The stovetop method gives the cook maximum control. You can watch the foam, adjust the simmer, test texture every 15 minutes, and decide exactly when to add aromatics, salt, or acidic ingredients. For brothy beans, baked bean preparations, and recipes where bean liquor is part of the final dish, this control is valuable. A Dutch oven or heavy stockpot with a tight lid works best because it buffers temperature swings and reduces evaporation. At altitude, I recommend starting with beans sorted and rinsed, soaking them in salted water for 8 to 12 hours when possible, draining, then simmering in fresh water with enough headroom for expansion.

The key with stovetop cooking is maintaining a true simmer, not a rolling boil. Aggressive boiling breaks skins, especially on black beans and cannellini, while under-heating prolongs the cook. Keep beans covered by at least 1 to 2 inches of water throughout cooking. Many mountain cooks need to add near-boiling water two or three times during a long batch; adding cold water can slow the pot and toughen skins temporarily. A lid set slightly ajar usually balances steam retention with boil-over control. For aromatic flavoring, onions, garlic, bay, and chile can go in early, but tomatoes, citrus, and vinegar should wait until beans are nearly tender.

Stovetop drawbacks are time and inconsistency. An altitude batch of unsoaked pintos may take three hours or more, and even soaked beans can vary widely because bean age is rarely labeled. Energy use is higher, and electric coil or weak gas burners can struggle to hold a steady low simmer. Still, for cooks who want tactile control and are making soups, stews, cassoulet-style dishes, or freezer batches, stovetop remains the most flexible option.

Pressure cooker beans at altitude: why they often perform better

A pressure cooker solves the main altitude problem by increasing the cooking temperature. At full pressure, water can reach roughly 240°F to 250°F depending on the device, far above the local boiling point in an open pot. That higher temperature speeds starch gelatinization and cell-wall breakdown, so beans soften faster and more consistently. In my own altitude tests, soaked black beans that needed about 95 to 120 minutes on the stovetop at 5,500 feet reached a creamy texture in about 18 to 22 minutes at high pressure with a natural release. Chickpeas that stretched beyond two hours open-pot were reliably tender in 35 to 45 minutes.

Pressure cookers also reduce evaporation, preserve more bean liquor, and minimize the need for babysitting. This is especially useful in dry climates, where stovetop pots lose water quickly. For meal prep, pressure cooking is the most dependable route to weeknight beans. It is also the easiest method for beans with thick skins, such as chickpeas and large limas. Stovetop pressure cookers generally reach and maintain slightly higher effective pressure than many electric multicookers, so they can finish beans faster. Electric models trade some speed for convenience and safety features, but both outperform open-pot cooking at altitude.

items.title: Tinkering with reveal.js: a slick, JavaScript-based, FOSS presentation framework
items.summary: Tinkering with reveal.js: a slick, JavaScript-based, FOSS presentation framework（来源：Hacker News）
items.content:
Tinkering with reveal.js: a slick, JavaScript-based, FOSS presentation framework

Published on: 2022-05-05 10:00:00 by Neil Brown

src="https://neilzone.co.uk/content/images/20220505220423-revealjs.png"

alt="Screenshot of the content available about decoded.legal/presentations: a slide with black text on a background of a mostly-transparent image of people in a large conference venue" />

Screenshot of the content available about

decoded.legal/presentations: a slide with black text on a background of

a mostly-transparent image of people in a large conference

I have wanted to play with <a

href="https://revealjs.com/">reveal.js for a while, as a way of

improving the look of my presentation slides, and I’ve finally got round

to doing so.

I am impressed. Very impressed.

Impress (LibreOffice),

pandoc, and beamer

Since switching to Linux full-time, and really disliking

Impress , the presentation tool in the LibreOffice suite, I

have been writing presentations in markdown, and then using

pandoc to convert them into beamer , and then

convert them to PDF.

I love the simplicity of writing content in markdown, as I can focus

on what I am including in the slides, rather than on their formatting,

which is handled by a template.

But - for me at least - getting the template correct in

pandoc / beamer was harder work than I wanted. I

had to accept a number of compromises, and while my slides were still

adequate they were not what I wanted.

Enter reveal.js.

reveal.js uses a similar approach: write your slide content, and then

use templates to control slide rendering.

Fortunately, reveal.js uses html, css, and JavaScript, and I can

adjust those to do what I want far more easily than I can with

pandoc . It took about 10 minutes from downloading the basic

files to have a theme looking how I wanted it.

It’s an open source project, and doesn’t require you to host your

slides on someone else’s system. In fact, I have stuck with the <a

href="https://revealjs.com/installation/">Basic setup and, while the

Advanced setup (running a local webserver) is “recommended”, I haven’t

found anything I’m missing out on yet. It says that the Advanced setup

is required for external markdown content; I just write the content in

markdown (in Apostrophe ), and then paste it into the

reveal.js index file, and that works fine.

I spent an evening reading the

docs - time well spent - and experimenting with different features,

and was quickly producing presentations which look more than good enough

for my needs with very little effort.

I have bought the video course, as a means of supporting the

developer, and I look forward to watching that when I get a few spare

hours. (It’s worth learning how to use tools well, IMHO, especially

since I make my living from them.)

Videos, images, fancy backgrounds, nice transitions - they are all

supported, although, clearly, I will be using them sparingly. I like

slides to be a backdrop to what I am saying, not the main feature.

It also has a feature I really missed from my PDF-based approach:

speaker view! I like to see what the next slide/build is going to be, as

that helps me with my presentation, and being able to see a clock, to

keep track of time, is also welcome.

(Do I sound like a bit of a fanboy? Probably, and deservedly so…)

Because it is html/css/js based, it means that I can upload (public)

presentations to my webserver, and people can interact with them,

letting them click through the slides as if they were me giving the

presentation. No more reliance on static PDF downloads (although those

can be generated simply too), although it does require JavaScript to be

enabled. I’ve put an

example presentation online so you can see what I mean. Nifty,

right?! (And if you access the site via Tor Browser, you’ll get

redirected automatically to the .onion version of the site, and the

slides will be served up within Tor.)

On the downside, some of the features I want to use do require me to

switch from markdown to html - for example, using fragments, to “build”

slides with multiple stages, which is reasonably common - but I can cope

with that, and I will use espanso to automate it.

Firefox v Brave

Update: this is out of date. It turns out that I needed to use a

more recent version of Firefox than the one in Debian stable. Using

that, I’ve no need for Brave.

My go-to browser is Firefox. I have used it for many, many years, and

Sadly, it does not render reveal.js slides well. Transitions have a

noticeable lag, and the overall experience is not good.

I’ve been using Brave for a few months now, for running Microsoft

Teams in-browser. On a whim, I opened one of my reveal.js presentations

in Brave, and boy was it good. Absolutely no lag at all, and

everything was so much snappier.

I do wonder for how much longer I will use Firefox, to be honest; I

can see a move to Brave on the cards.

One thing I still need to work on is how to run a reveal.js

presentation in Brave, when I am sharing the Brave tab on a Teams (and

perhaps other?) conference call. Normally, I just load the slides in

Brave, hit “F” to go full screen, and off I go. However, when I am

sharing the tab via Teams, there is a warning message at the top of the

screen, reminding me that I am sharing the tab, and this prevents me

from going into full screen mode. I suspect there is a solution out

there for this, but I don’t yet know what that is.

items.content:
Methane-consuming organisms create nanowires that grow on electrode – and can generate a small amount of electricity

09 November 2026

Research news item

Certain microorganisms (anaerobic methanotrophic archaea, or ANME) consume methane and convert it into electricity, as research conducted four years ago by microbiologist Cornelia Welte of Radboud University revealed. New research by Welte and her colleagues now shows that these methane-consuming organisms do this by producing nanowires through which they can transmit the electricity they generate. The researchers have also succeeded in cultivating these specific microorganisms in almost pure form in the lab.

It was already known that microorganisms other than ANME develop nanowires, but it was not yet known whether ANME did too. Welte: ‘We have been searching for these answers for so long, and now we can see that these microorganisms feed electricity back to an electrode via their self-made nanowires. We already strongly suspected this would be the case, and have now been able to visualise it beautifully under a special microscope.’

Welte’s research revealed that ANME love growing on an electrode through which a small voltage is passing. In fact, they enjoy it so much that they grow much faster there than they do in the wild. ‘ANME divide once a month when they’re out in ditches and trenches, but on the electrodes in our lab, they divide once every five days. So that works very well.’

In Welte’s lab, the microorganisms grow in a small vessel containing water. They are fed methane and attach themselves to an electrode in the water, where they multiply. They also send electrons to the electrode, which means they generate a small amount of current. This current could be used, for example, to produce hydrogen, although, according to Welte, this is still a long way off. ‘In theory, the microorganisms can generate electricity from methane using a small amount of voltage, much more efficiently than, for example, a electrolyzer can. That could be a practical application in about twenty years’ time, but for now, we are mainly looking at how these ANME work at a fundamental level.’

The researchers also succeeded in culturing the ANME in such a way that 95 per cent of the microbial community consisted of these ANME. This had never been achieved before. ‘If you have such a pure culture, you can study these microorganisms much more effectively than when everything is growing together. We achieved this through collaboration with various partners, including researchers from Yale.’

Welte points out that this technique could become highly relevant in the future. ‘As natural resources run out, we will have to find new, energy-efficient ways to generate electricity. This could be achieved by using microorganisms. But at present, the technique is still far too expensive and complex. Hopefully, it can be made more efficient in the future. With this research, we’ve taken another small step in that direction.’

items.summary: How we made table parsing 4× faster with DFlash（来源：Hacker News）
items.content:
Back to the main blog How we made table parsing 4x faster with DFlash

Joon Kim, Jing Reyhan, Devin Logan

Tables are the biggest latency bottleneck in document parsing . A dense table can take thousands of tokens to represent in HTML, including markup for every row and cell. Every token adds latency, and with standard decoding, each new token takes another pass through the model.

Any processing latency delays the work that depends on the data downstream, from matching bank transactions against a ledger to checking procedure codes on a medical bill or verifying carton counts against a freight manifest.

Some tables are highly repetitive: a credit card statement might list the same merchant and amount dozens of times, with only the date changing. But many tables, like financial summaries, are dense with numbers that follow no pattern, and a general speedup solution has to handle those too.

Our first approach to improving latency was n-gram speculation, which drafts upcoming tokens from earlier output so the model can verify several at once. n-gram made table parsing around 1.5–2× faster, but we didn't see latency gains on non-repetitive tables. We switched to DFlash, which uses a trained drafter instead, to better handle all table types. With an off-the-shelf DFlash drafter, median Light Table latency fell from 3.35 seconds to 1.76 seconds on a single H100.

After fine-tuning, acceptance length rose from 6.73 to 12.48 tokens per verification pass giving us a 4x speedup.

Median Light Table latency on one H100, with tables averaging about 100 cells. Trained DFlash had the lowest latency at all six concurrency levels. Compared with speculation off, it was 4.40× faster at one concurrent request, peaked at 4.74× faster at two, and was 1.90× faster at 32. Base DFlash was 1.91× faster at one request and 1.13× faster at 32. What is speculative decoding?

LLMs generate text one token at a time. Each token requires a full forward pass through the model, and each pass waits on the one before it. This results in high latency when parsing long outputs like tables.

Play animation Speculative decoding can reduce this latency by guessing ahead. A drafter proposes several tokens, and the target model checks the sequence in one pass. If the first five draft tokens match what the target would choose and the sixth diverges, we keep the first five, use the target's token at position six, and discard the rest of the draft. This saves time when drafting and verifying the block costs less than generating those tokens one at a time.

Play animation Acceptance length measures how many tokens each verification pass advances the output. A longer accepted sequence reduces the number of target-model passes needed to finish. When guesses fail early, drafting and verification can cost more than standard decoding.

Why n-gram speculation works best on repetitive tables

Table HTML repeats the same tags across rows, and some tables repeat cell values too. We started with n-gram speculation to see how much of the next row we could draft from earlier output without training a separate model. As the table model generated HTML, we indexed sequences of tokens it had already emitted in a trie. At each decoding step, we looked up the most recent tokens in that history. If the same sequence had appeared before, we took the tokens that followed it and proposed them as the next part of the output. Drafting was a lookup, with no extra model pass.

This worked well on tables with repeated values as well as repeated markup. For example, if a statement lists the same merchant and amount several times, an earlier row can supply much of the next one. But a table can have a perfectly regular grid and a different value in every cell. N-gram might correctly draft the opening <td> tag, then copy an amount from an earlier row. Verification stops as soon as the amount diverges, so the drafter gets little benefit from the markup it guessed correctly later in the row.

In earlier production observations, n-gram averaged about five tokens per verification pass. We wanted a drafter that could make progress even when the next cell value hadn't appeared before.

Play animation How DFlash speeds up table parsing by drafting tokens in parallel

DFlash uses hidden states from several layers of the table model to condition a small drafter. We used a 16-position block. The first position is anchored by a token the target has already produced, and bidirectional attention lets the drafter predict the remaining positions in parallel. The table model then verifies the proposed tokens.

Since DFlash drafts from the model's representation of the input and output so far, it can propose a cell value that hasn't appeared in an earlier row.

N-gram DFlash How it drafts Finds a matching sequence in earlier output and reuses what followed it. Uses the table model's hidden states to predict a block of upcoming tokens. Training requirements No training needed. The lookup history builds as the model generates tokens. A compatible pre-trained drafter. Drafting costs A lookup in the token history. One forward pass through a small draft model per block. What improves the draft More useful matches in the token history. Fine-tuning the drafter on outputs from the model that will verify its predictions. Off-the-shelf DFlash nearly halved median latency

Before training a DFlash head of our own, we tried one trained for the base model. We wanted to see whether it could still predict the next tokens after we had fine-tuned the target model to generate table HTML. We tested on a single H100 using a mix of real-world tables from business documents, averaging about 100 cells per table. With one request in flight, median latency fell from 3.35 to 1.76 seconds on Light Table and from 3.85 to 2.01 seconds on Performance Table, compared with speculation off. That's about 1.9× faster on each model.

items.summary: Our Survey of Early Career Mathematicians（来源：Hacker News）
items.content:
[This is a guest post by Anna Brandenberger , Hanna Mularczyk , and Dora Woodruff (MIT). This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

In late September and early October, we distributed a survey of early career mathematicians. Our goals were to take a “temperature check” of the community, and to give early career mathematicians a centralized, targeted platform to share their views on AI (the survey was not a rigorous data analysis effort). The personal stakes are highest for grad students and postdocs, who face job insecurity and funding instability, so it’s important that our voices are taken into account. We worry that our concerns will be deprioritized, or even misrepresented, without collective resources like this survey.

On October 29th, we posted the results of this survey to the arXiv (history and overview). In the end, over 260 mathematicians filled out the survey, representing around 60 institutions and at least 5 countries. Many of them left free responses in addition to answering the multiple choice questions.

This blog post is an invitation to take a look at the survey results. Some of the results surprised and/or dismayed us: in particular, Question 3.2, Question 3.3, Question 5.2, and Question 6.1, which concern career outlook and research motivation. It’s also important to point out that nearly all of the responses were collected before October 6th, capturing a sample of thoughts from a specific context: we nervously wonder how different this data would look today. As journals, hiring committees, and faculty members make decisions about the future, we urge them to take these survey results into account — and to continue fostering discussions between senior and junior mathematicians.

IBM plans to bring Anthropic’s Claude Mythos cyber reasoning into IBM Concert

Frontier AI cyber reasoning meets enterprise exposure management to help uncover unknown vulnerabilities and accelerate remediation at AI scale.

Published 09 November 2026

IBM Concert plans to bring Anthropic’s Claude Mythos’ cyber reasoning into enterprise security to help organizations discover previously unknown vulnerabilities, validate real-world exploitability and accelerate remediation.

The planned capability will combine Mythos-powered AI code scanning with Concert Protect’s enterprise exposure management capabilities, helping security teams to uncover weaknesses traditional scanners miss, determine which pose real risk and generate fixes for developer approval.

IBM has an established strategic relationship with Anthropic and has partnered with the company on cybersecurity initiatives, including Project Glasswing. While IBM’s work through Project Glasswing focused on internal security research and evaluation, the planned Concert Protect integration represents a new step toward bringing Claude Mythos’ capabilities to enterprise customers through a governed operations platform. This combines advanced capabilities into established vulnerability and exposure management workflows.

Alongside Red Hat Lightwell for open-source fixes, IBM Concert Protect with Anthropic’s Claude Mythos is intended to help clients discover, validate and remediate vulnerabilities in their own code.

AI is changing the cybersecurity equation

Frontier AI is transforming cybersecurity. Advanced models can analyze complex codebases, discover unknown vulnerabilities at considerable scale, and uncover attack paths conventional scanners may overlook.

Anthropic’s research with Claude Mythos has described how AI can identify weaknesses that were not surfaced by traditional testing and expert review.

Traditional scanners largely rely on known signatures and published vulnerabilities. But as AI accelerates discovery, organizations can no longer depend on waiting for CVE identifiers or severity scores.

The bottleneck is no longer finding vulnerabilities. It is determining which can actually be exploited and fixing them before attackers do.

Bringing frontier AI discovery into enterprise exposure management

By embedding Claude Mythos into Concert Protect, IBM intends to bring advanced AI cyber reasoning directly into established enterprise security workflows.

The planned AI code scanning capability would analyze customer-selected repositories to help uncover unknown weaknesses, including complex logic flaws and potential zero-days that conventional scanners may miss.

Rather than introducing another standalone tool, Mythos-powered findings would enter Concert Protect’s existing vulnerability management lifecycle alongside traditional scanner results, unifying discovery with enterprise context, evidence-based validation and remediation.

Scan. Prove. Fix. From discovery to verified remediation

The planned offering brings together three complementary capabilities:

Scan: Discover what traditional scanners miss.

Claude Mythos would reason across customer-selected application code to help identify previously unknown vulnerabilities, including weaknesses without existing signatures or CVE records.

Prove: Validate what attackers can actually exploit.

Concert Protect’s Proof of Exploitability capability helps teams move beyond severity scores and predicted risk. By analyzing code, configuration, and infrastructure context, it can evaluate viable exploitation paths and provide supporting evidence.

Fix: Accelerate remediation with developer-approved changes.

IBM Concert Protect, together with Red Hat Lightwell, helps with risk-based vulnerability remediation by identifying and prioritizing exploitable risks, leveraging trusted backported open-source fixes, generating targeted remediation changes, and helping developers to validate, review, and approve fixes through automated pull-request workflows.

Together, these capabilities connect discovery, validation, and remediation in one enterprise-grade platform.

A new era of enterprise exposure management

As AI transforms vulnerability discovery, enterprises need more than powerful scanners. They need to determine which risks matter and act at enterprise scale.

Discover what others miss. Prove what matters. Fix it autonomously.

Sony’s new PlayStation Portal handheld includes ‘additional’ internal storage

The Japan-only model arrives on December 10th in a midnight black color scheme.

The Japan-only model arrives on December 10th in a midnight black color scheme.

by Tom Warren

Nov 9, 2026, 4:23 PM UTC

Tom Warren is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad , who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.

Sony is launching a new version of its PlayStation Portal exclusively in Japan next month. The updated model will launch in the midnight black color option we’ve seen before , and will include “additional” internal storage for future-looking features.

It’s the additional internal storage that’s the surprise change to this particular model, which will be locked to Japanese language options and can only be used with a PlayStation account registered in Japan. Sony says the extra storage is for “future functionality” that it will announce once these features are finalized.

Sony is also renaming this particular Portal from PlayStation Portal Remote Player to PlayStation Portal Player. The name change, combined with extra internal storage, seems to suggest that this particular model might get access to streaming apps.

The existing PlayStation Portal doesn’t support streaming apps like YouTube, Disney Plus, or Netflix, and is primarily designed to stream PS5 games from a console or the cloud. The PlayStation Portal isn’t powerful enough to play PlayStation games locally, but extra storage could also let you sync media for offline playback.

This Japan-only PlayStation Portal is launching on December 10th, priced at 39,980 yen (around $253).

Medium is launching a new note-taking app called TK

The company is betting that the future of blogging looks a lot like group chats.

The company is betting that the future of blogging looks a lot like group chats.

by David Pierce

Nov 9, 2026, 3:04 PM UTC

Think of TK as Google Docs meets group chats, meets blogging. Image: David Pierce / The Verge

David Pierce is editor-at-large and Vergecast co-host with over a decade of experience covering consumer tech. Previously, at Protocol, The Wall Street Journal, and Wired.

For the first time ever, Medium is becoming more than just a blogging platform. The company is launching a new app, called TK , that combines note taking and journaling with something resembling a private social network. The app is meant to get you writing more, and help you share that writing with friends and fans. And it’s part of a much bigger idea about blogging, and a much broader thesis about the state of the internet.

“I don’t think we’ve actually had a launch of anything important since 2017,” Medium CEO Tony Stubblebine tells me over Zoom, a few days ahead of the company’s biggest launch in apparently almost a decade. That was when Medium’s then-CEO, Ev Williams, decided to quit chasing ad dollars and become a subscription business. “It’s clear that the broken system is ad-driven media on the internet,” Williams wrote at the time . “It simply doesn’t serve people. In fact, it’s not designed to.” Medium began charging for access to most content. “We got out of the attention economy,” Stubblebine says now.

The trend Williams saw back then, though, has only accelerated and metastasized. AI companies are hoovering up any content they can get their hands on, legality be damned; search engines and chatbots are sending less and less traffic back to the web. Medium, like most websites on the internet, relies on Google for a huge portion of its traffic — in the time of Google Zero , that’s an existential risk. “When Google started taking away all the traffic,” Stubblebine says, “what I told them is that this hurts us, but it also hurts you, because I’ll just tell you what my product roadmap is going to do: I’m going to switch to private blogging… We’re just going to take everything underground.”

TK is for writing — but it’s also for taking quick notes and finding them later. Image: David Pierce / The Verge

All of which brings us back to TK, an app and network that has no use or need for Google referrals. The idea behind TK is fairly straightforward: It’s a barebones note-taking app, with emphasis on daily journal-style notes and longer-form writing. The app itself is nice enough, like an ultra-minimalist take on Evernote, but it’s the stuff around the writing that has Stubblebine most excited.

For one thing, you can point an AI model at your writing, and use it to help organize or make sense of all the notes you’ve been taking, by searching through your notes or asking for feedback on your writing. “TK” is both the name of the app and a shortcut in it: type the letters (which writers use frequently as a placeholder — they’re easy to find later, since the letters T and K hardly ever appear next to each other otherwise) and you can summon the model to fill in a bit of information for you. Stubblebine refers to “Unix pipes” a few times in our conversation, and his idea is to use the large language models to do some of the grunt work of both creating and managing notes.

Libraries — private blogs — are the core social concept of TK. Screenshot: David Pierce / The Verge

Once you’ve written something – and Stubblebine emphasizes that it doesn’t have to be a blog post — you can then share it however you like. You can share it via links or email the way you’d share a Google Doc, and collaborators can write, comment, and leave emoji reactions. You can also add your writing to what TK calls Libraries. Stubblebine calls the Libraries concept “private blogging,” which is a good metaphor. The early Libraries I’ve seen in the app are mostly centered around a topic, and people can contribute their writing on that topic. There’s no public face to any of it; it’s just a blog for and by its authors. Sometimes a few of them, sometimes a few hundred. There are groups sharing their ongoing book projects, swapping recipes, and posting poetry drafts, all for the eyes of only the other people in the group. It’s blogging meets group chats.

This concept of private blogging is a big part of the future of Medium. “Medium is, at some level, performative,” Stubblebine says. “You have to want to share yourself with the world.” But in a post-Google world, he says, that’s essentially impossible. TK doesn’t measure pageviews or reward authors for getting traffic. “This is a community that’s going to give you feedback and encouragement,” Stubblebine says. “It’s not about the drive to be noticed.” Features like this, he says, are coming to the broader Medium platform soon.

TK is now available, for free, via apps for the web, Android, and iOS. (Stubblebine says a native desktop app is also coming soon.) If TK works, though, it could be a crucial new way for Medium to make money. Obviously, Stubblebine says, there are ways to make money from private and paywalled content. That’s the newsletter business. But also, he wonders, what if there’s a way to package up all the best stuff from the Recipe Box library and charge people, or AI agents, for access? “The generic web is getting dumber and dumber,” Stubblebine says. If AI is the future, “it needs to be based on this layer of human intelligence.” And all that intelligence might be better off outside the confines of the Google algorithm.
